utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honour. For the Defence of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, myself, counsel, and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to welcome everybody in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, and the accused, and everybody else. We have two witnesses to hear today, one witness who is continuing his testimony from yesterday, plus a second witness. I hope that we'll get through everything as scheduled by 1.45. Would Madam Usher please introduce the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I hope you had a good evening last night. We're going to continue the proceedings this morning, but rest assured that we will get through your testimony in the course of the morning. And without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution, and they had several additional questions to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Mundis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday when we adjourned, you had just told us about an encounter that you had in the primary school in Mehurici with the person whom had been identified to you as Ramadan. Do you recall the approximate time period when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, once again, roughly, sometime in July, maybe a month after their arrival. I can't be certain, but I assume that was when that happened, in 1992. July, perhaps August. Maybe it would -- it might have been August. A lot of time has gone by since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that we're absolutely clear, sir, this was the only time that you ever spoke to or had any encounters with any of these Arabs from the period 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only time. I didn't have occasion to contact -- have any contacts with those people. The position I occupied, I didn't have an opportunity. I didn't want to. And as I said, I felt uncomfortable in their presence, so I didn't have any more contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now just ask you a couple of questions, sir, about whether or not during the period, again, the second half of 1992 and 1993: How frequently would you see these people in the area of Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I would go there every day to the regional staff in Mehurici, I would see them very frequently. But when I went to the school building, I would do the job I'd come to do and go back to my village. So I would just see them going in and out of the school building and the school courtyard. I knew nothing else about their movements or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, sir, when you say you went every day to the regional staff, how -- and you would see them very frequently, what time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, it was the period of time -- there seems to be something with the interpretation. Let me repeat. Well, it was the time when they first appeared in our area until the brigade had been formed. So it was 1992, sometime from the time of their arrival, up until August, thereabouts, that's what I would see them around in front of the school, going in and out of the school building. I didn't see them anywhere else at that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall approximately when these Arabs left the school in Mehurici and went to the area known as Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about that yesterday, and I said that they left the premises during the period when the units of the 1st Battalion came to be in the school. They were soldiers who were from the neighbouring municipality of Kotor Varos and Siprige. And as they weren't able to find -- they weren't able to be there together, I don't think they liked the conduct of the units. They sang and so on. So I think they left of their own free will and went to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is do you recall approximately time period that was, what month and year?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. It has been 11 years since then. I'd be very willing to tell you, but unfortunately I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn to the final few questions that I have. You told us that you were a member of the 306th Mountain Brigade until 19 November 1993 when you received a work obligation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this work obligation required you to return to the career of teaching?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your experience in the 306th Mountain Brigade, towards the latter part of 1993, was it common for soldiers in your brigade to be demobilised by way of receiving work obligations?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't customary for people from the army to be demobilised and be assigned work obligations. We had work obligations. I know about our department. I don't know about the other departments. We who worked in the education sector, in schools, and so on. But as I say, a lot of time had gone by when our children didn't go to school, so the civilian authorities sat and had a meeting somewhere, and I suppose decided that it would have a serious impact on future generations if from May 1992 right up to 1993, which means more than a year, a year and a half, children didn't go to school, that this would have far-reaching consequences, adverse consequences on the young people in the country as a whole. So I suppose that since the basic elementary conditions did exist, they tried to organise tuition wherever possible. So as I say, I don't know about the other branches, but in our area, in my department, people who they thought would do the job best and were ready to work under such conditions were given a work obligation to go ahead and teach. And that's how I came to teach in the village of Gluha Bukavica, nine kilometres to the north of Mehurici, and I taught children from the first year of school to the fourth year of primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, my final question, if you know, you say people who they thought would do the job best and were ready to work under such conditions, do you know approximately how many people fit into that category?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how many people would be in that category, but I do know that on the day I started to work that I was demobilised and Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond another colleague teacher of mine. Later on, some others came in, but I can't give you their names and when they actually came, but there were two people, myself and the chemistry teacher, we were mobilised on that same day and took up our jobs the very next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a clarification question, sir. On page 6, line 1, it says "we were mobilised on that same day."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Demobilised. Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, at this time, the Prosecution has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence. Re-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jasarevic, I just have a few follow-up questions for you.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Edina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your regional staff was in the school in Mehurici. So tell me who mobilised the facilities and premises used later by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that exactly, who mobilised or requisitioned those premises. I know we entered them, but in the municipality, there was a municipal secretariat for national defence. That was a civilian authority which took care about all the military records, so I assume it could have been the municipal secretariat for national defence attached to the municipality itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, asked by my learned colleague, you spoke about how far people had been equipped or trained to perform their duties and how many people had had military training beforehand. Tell me, now, please, in view of the many problems that there were with people who lacked training and the cadres that you spoke about, in the 306th Brigade, for instance, were men trained? And if so, who conducted the training?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in the 306th Brigade, there was some training which was conducted by the officers of the 306th Brigade. I know that there was a training plan compiled by one of the organs of the brigade. I don't remember exactly. But I do know that the soldiers who, in their free time, when they came back from their positions, would undergo training, usually in the places they lived in. I can tell you about my own village where I lived. Training was conducted at one of the areas around there, so there were soldiers who had just joined the army, joined up, and didn't know how to handle weapons. So the basic issue was to teach them how to handle weapons. And in addition to that, they took care to see that the soldiers had elementary training in the laws and customs of war, for example, and respect for those provisions. So I do think there was this kind of training, and there were plans that were compiled and devised. And yes, the brigade did organise training sessions in the manner in which I have described; that is to say, the training took place in the places they lived and worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, were there any foreigners, especially these foreigners from Poljanice, for example, did they conduct training of the members of the 306th Brigade at any point in time to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw them do any training. And to the best of my knowledge, they never trained people in the brigade. And I can say specifically for my own village that this was done by a lower ranking officer who would take the men up on the slopes, and then that's where it would take place. So every village or every unit or every officer or NCO would be in charge of training men in his unit as provided for by the programme. But there was absolutely no question of this being done by any foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, did you also receive orders from the superior command of the 3rd Corps about the necessity for conducting training in all sectors of work in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: Once the 306th Brigade had been set up, the principle of the chain of command was set up in the army so that the units lower down were subordinated to the superior command, superior units. And everything we talked about yesterday, we did exclusively under the command of the 3rd Corps. Therefore, everything that was done was done on the basis of documents, at least that's what I was informed about. And I think I saw some of them anyway. But as I say, on the basis of documents coming down and orders issued by the command of the 3rd Corps. So when it came to training and all other aspects of military life and sectors, we wanted the job to be done well, to see that the war ended in the best possible way, without people being under threat too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, yesterday asked by my learned colleague, you spoke about the fact that you informed people and gave them the rudimentary knowledge they needed about humanitarian law and war law as you, as an intellectual understood it, and as far as you were able to teach them based on your general education. Now what I'm interested in is this: What was the relationship between the brigade and the army itself? That is to say the 3rd Corps, what was that are attitude generally speaking towards crimes, the perpetration of crimes? Were there any orders connected to that and what measures were taken, what steps were taken?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the positions of my duties, and I've already explained what my duties were, as men and individuals, we were absolutely astounded by the war and what was happening. So certain orders were issued and instructions given as to what should be done to people and whether they were members of our brigade or not, something along those lines. I can't remember exactly. But it was the position taken by the brigade and our command, categoric position, that these crimes had to be punished, the perpetrators had to be brought to justice, and that the people that suffered at their hands must be helped as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to other crimes such as theft, looting, and things of that kind, do you happen to know yourself what the orders were to prevent anything like that? And do you know yourself how the organs of the 306th Brigade in charge of affairs of that kind, what their conduct was, how they behaved and what they did, if anything like that should happen?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke yesterday about the morale of our units, moral guidance they were given, and I said that there was no idea of revenge in the minds of the men of the 306th Brigade. I can't say for everyone, but our men were not prone to theft, looting, and retaliation of that kind. Now, if an incident like that did happen, if an individual soldier did go round thieving and looting, he would be sanctioned, he would be punished. Now, my department has no records of that. That wasn't our job. But I think that all the people against whom proceedings were taken, I think there was a security service and that records of that kind exist in the security service of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn to the other Defence team. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no questions from us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges have a few questions to ask you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I want to come back to something you said yesterday. You said a number of things on destruction of property, of villages, and a comparison was made between villages that were attacked by the Croat forces and villages attacked by the ABiH Army forces. And you said in particular, I've seen Bandol and Velika Bukovica, two villages that were taken by the Croat forces, I've seen destructions there, and I can say -- I can tell you that I've never seen such destructions in villages taken by the -- my own army. Is this a fair summary of what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I said that the job I did up until the 19th of Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond November 1993 was in the social services, and I moved around in the region of Guca Gora. So I say during that period of time, that is really how it was. The houses hadn't been destroyed, so that was a period of about two months. During that period of time, during those two months, the houses were left intact. They were standing and they hadn't been destroyed or destructed. So it is my general position that during those two months the situation was really the way I described it. Later on, I left to take up my own work assignments, and I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt your statement, Witness, in that respect, and that's not the point of my question. You mentioned yesterday, indeed, Guca Gora. This morning you said "I visited the Guca Gora area." What other villages did you visit in that time?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I think that the terrain I moved around and the direction of my movements from the brigade to the centre for giving assistance to those families, I had to pass through Guca Gora every day. As to the other villages, I didn't tour them. I didn't have a chance to go round those villages, nor did I have time to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So, for instance, Maline, which is very close to Guca Gora, you did not visit Maline, I understand now?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to Maline. That wasn't the road to Krpeljici, the route was from the warehouse and the place where our storage space was located across to Guca Gora. So there was no need for me to go to Maline. I went via Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And I take it that you did not visit villages on the other side of the River Bila, like, for instance, Cukle or Susanj, that kind of places?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to those villages, and I stated the reason. And I said yesterday, I gave you the exact date when by an order I was transferred to the area facing the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor. I suppose somebody else did that. And if he comes into court here, we'll be able to provide you with that information. I wasn't in a physical position to go there because I did other work. And when I returned in August at the social services, there was so much work I was inundated. So it wasn't up to me, my job, to visit those villages. I assume someone else did, but I don't know exactly who. I did not, as I say. I had other work assignments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This has now become much clearer to me. I have a second question on the elementary school in Mehurici. You told us that a number of Croats came from Maline and were housed in the school for several weeks, and you were very busy providing them, organising support and help to them, for instance in the manner of food. If I understood you well, you came in Mehurici the day after this group of Croats came in the school. Is that right? Or could you indicate a different day?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Mehurici at the time when that group of Croats arrived and when they were assigned the premises. I received an order from my superior the next day, so I think I was in Mehurici then, and I think it says so in my statement. But I wasn't given a concrete work assignment. That came the following day. And I received the assignment that I stated during my testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the school on the day the Croats arrived already? Did you see the school on that day?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the school that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And were the Croats already in the school at that moment? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I learned of this, they had already been put up in the sports hall. They were in the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because we have heard a witness in January, on the 20th of January of this year, and this witness told us that when he came into the school, he was one of the Croats, he saw a flag hanging out of the school, a black flag from the third floor. Do you remember ever having seen such a flag, a black flag hanging out of some window in the school?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke a moment ago about the fact that the units who were made up of the Arabs, that that unit had left and gone to the camp in Poljanice with all their characteristic features and things that they had brought with them. But as far as I remember, there was never a black flag. No black flag at all in the school. All there was was one which belonged to the 306th Brigade which was there, so there was no black flag. I did not see a black flag at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Maybe I can show you a picture of the school revealing -- maybe I could show you a picture taken of the school. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 28.1 on which the witness has indicated where the flag was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we will go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my question concerns the Red Cross. Yesterday in response to a question, you said -- or you mentioned the Red Cross, and you said - and I will summarise you - you said that when the people arrived, you and your superior were obliged to inform the Red Cross of the fact. And this is what you allegedly did, and you also added that the Red Cross arrived eight or ten days later. So according to my calculations, you were there on the 8th of June. If add on ten days that brings us to the 18th of June. So the Red Cross arrived on the 18th or the 19th of June. You said that Red Cross representatives had no comments or Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond objections to make. Were you present when the Red Cross representatives arrived on the 18th or 19th of June?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there when the Red Cross arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were there. When they arrived, where did Red Cross representatives see the people?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they arrived at the site, they saw the people, the people who were kept in the sports hall. That's where they had been kept throughout the entire period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a witness who appears to have given us a different version, a contradictory version. He said that they had been taken to another building and that that is where they met Red Cross representatives. What could you say about this slight contradiction? To refresh your memory, I will quote what this person said very rapidly. A certain number of soldiers from the civilian police came with a list containing the names of various persons. All those on the list had to leave the sports hall and were taken to another building close by. There were other Croats there, including women. I'd like to be clear about this. The Red Cross representatives, did they see people in the school or outside the school? You're telling us that you were present. So please, clarify this for us. And I'd like to remind you that you have taken the solemn declaration and said that you will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the school and spoke to the people in the hall, in the sports hall. I don't know whether they spoke to these other prisoners in another building. I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Prosecution have any questions that arise from the Judges' questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this concludes your testimony. Thank you for having come to testify at the request of the Defence. You've testified about what occurred in 1992 and 1993, and we thank you for that. We wish you a good trip home. And I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm addressing the Defence now. We have one last witness for this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Hockic is waiting to be called into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will wait for him to come in. How much time do you think you will need for his examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I probably won't need more than half an hour, but I have a series of documents that I have prepared for the witness. So we will probably need just as much time to examine the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for this good news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence, for Defence counsel for one of the accused. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you please tell me your first and last names, your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mustafa Hockic. I was born on the 9th of May in 1947 in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What do you do at the moment? Do you hold a professional position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a professor. I am the deputy director of the cantonal administration for civilian protection in Travnik at the time -- at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1992 and 1993, what professional post did you hold and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I was employed in the municipal secretariat for national defence, and I worked as the assistant chief of the secretariat for national defence. And I was involved in civilian protection affairs and general affairs. I also acted as chief of the municipal civilian protection staff in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified about the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993 before a national or international court? Or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence, I'd like to provide you with some information about the procedure we will be following here. As you have said, this is the first time that you will be testifying. And since this will be your first time, I must provide you with some information. You will first have to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel for one of the accused. Defence counsel are sitting to your left. Their examination-in-chief should take about half an hour, but it might take a little longer since certain documents might be presented to you. After this stage, you will have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution, who are to your right. They will conduct what we call the cross-examination. You will notice that the questions they put to you won't be of the same kind since the questions that Defence counsel puts to you must not be leading, whereas according to the common-law system leading questions are permitted in the course of cross-examination. After the Prosecution has examined you, Defence may re-examine you. The Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions at any point in time. Usually, there are three of us, but one is absent for professional reasons. Usually we ask questions after both parties have finished with their questions. If a question appears complicated to you, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Perhaps you're not aware of this, but we don't have any written documents. We don't know exactly what you will be testifying about. And this is why what you say is so important. As a teacher, you are well aware of the importance of words. Take your time to understand the questions put to you, and try to answer the questions precisely. If you come across any difficulties, inform us of the fact. I'd also like to point out that as you have taken the solemn declaration and said that you will speak the truth, you should not give false testimony. False testimony is an offence which is punishable. You could be given a prison sentence. I'd also like to point out, although this shouldn't apply to you, I would also like to point out that if a witness's answer might provide information that could be used against the witness, according to our Rules, the witness can refuse to answer such a question. But the Trial Chamber can oblige -- can compel the witness to answer the question. If a Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond witness answers such a question, you should be aware of the fact that the witness is granted a form of immunity. So you can feel free to say whatever you have to say, especially since you have said that you will speak the truth. Generally speaking, this is how we will be proceeding today. Without wasting any more time, since we will be having our technical break at 10.30, I'll now give the floor to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hockic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to pause briefly after I have put my question to you. This will enable the interpreters to interpret my question and your answer. This will enable everyone to follow us, which is essential. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the work you did in 1992 and 1993. Could you please tell me whether before the war you performed any duties that had to do with the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, I worked in the Sipad work organisation. And just before the war, I moved to the secretariat for national defence, and I assumed the duties I mentioned. I forgot to mention, though, that in 1993 I was no longer the chief of the municipal staff, but I was a member -- I was the assistant chief for fire prevention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were a teacher by profession. Tell me where and when you completed the schools that qualified you to work as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I finished the university -- I graduated from the University of Political Science in Sarajevo. Should I say anything else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Tell me, what duties do you perform now?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Now I work as the deputy director in the cantonal administration for civilian protection in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could summarise, then, one could say that for the last ten years, you have been involved in working in the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, I could say that I have worked in the field of civilian protection for over 30 years now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The law on defence is already in evidence before this Chamber. Mr. Hockic, please tell me: The civilian protection forms which part of defence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The civilian protection comes under the laws that you mentioned. It comes under civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the superior organ?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence is the superior organ for the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent is the civilian protection linked to the municipal assembly? Or rather, in wartime conditions, to organs that replace the municipal assembly? Do these organs have any responsibility with regard to the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: In this case, it's the executive committee, or rather, the municipal government. Then there's the war presidency. And we were under these bodies as far as organisational matters are concerned. And the operation of the civilian protection in the Municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, could you briefly tell us what the main tasks of the civilian protection are.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Its main tasks involve protecting people and material and cultural goods in the case of natural disasters, in the case of accidents, or in the case of war and imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When carrying out these duties of yours, tell me whether the civilian protection takes any measures; and if so, could you mention some of the measures it takes to protect and save people and property.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: As a system, the civilian protection is involved firstly in self-protection, and then measures taken for civilian protection, and then it's involved in operating through civilian protection staffs, civilian protection units for general and specialised purposes. And it has its officials in that service for protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, in 1992 and 1993, when you were a member of the civilian protection staff, did the civilian protection in Travnik Municipality become involved in all the fields you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The municipality -- or rather, the civilian protection was involved in all the fields it should be involved in according to the law on defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the war, did you at any time become the organ -- the superior organ of some army units? Or the superior organ of the army as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No. We weren't the superior organ. They had their own command. We cooperated, if I could put it that way, with the army. And we were obliged to do so according to instructions issued in 1993 by the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, you have just answered my next question, in fact. Was the army ever the superior of the staffs, units, and organs of civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No, we were subordinated to the war presidency and the government, or rather the executive committee of the Municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were under the government and the war presidency of Travnik Municipality, did the government and the war presidency have the authority to determine what tasks you would have and to assign tasks to civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had such a authority on the basis of the law on defence that was in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, can you remember how many members there were in the civilian protection staff in Travnik Municipality in 1993 and how did they operate? Through which units and organs?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff of the civilian protection had 14 members, including the commander and the chief of the staff. And there was the professional service that had been ten members, too. And we were involved in all these tasks, or rather, the professional service was involved in technical issues, technical tasks for the needs of the staff. And we operated through 12 civilian protection staffs in local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the headquarters, the staffs in local communes, did the civilian protection staff have trained men who acted in the field or were these the direct tasks of the staff itself?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the staffs of the civilian protection in the local communes, we had about 130 civilian protection officials or representatives. They also operated in accordance with our decisions, orders, and instructions. And they worked in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the complexity of the task that you mentioned a while ago, was it important for the civilian protection staff to have professional officials and why was this important?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, the civilian defence staff was a professional and operative or operational organ, meaning that it dealt with professional matters and professional people were employed there. If it was the veterinary service and protection, you would have a vet there. If it meant first aid, you would have a doctor there. If it was fire prevention, you would have a fire prevention engineer employed in that sector, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, before the war and also during the war, in the civilian protection service, did you have a system of training at all? And if so, tell us please what kind of training it was.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: In the municipal civilian defence or civilian protection staff, we devoted special attention to training and education. We did this in the local communes, the civilian protection staff in local communes, in companies and enterprises. And the municipal civilian protection area so that at the very beginning of the war, that is to say in 1991, the entire staff spent time undergoing training for ten days in the federal centre for civilian protection which was located in Zemun. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the facts that have been repeated in this courtroom a number of times about the multiethnic composition of the work of your employees, what was the composition of the civilian protection people in 1992 and 1993, those who worked in that department?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: As you just said, we devoted considerable attention to the ethnic structure of distributing people to the organs of civilian protection. So in the municipal civilian protection staff in Travnik, for instance, in 1991 and 1992, there were six Bosniaks employed; six Croats; and two Serbs. And that fully reflected the ethnic structure of the population of the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I show you a series of documents, and I'd like to have your comments on those documents, tell me, please, what problems did you encounter, did the civilian protection staff encounter at the beginning of the war, and could you have foreseen the events and the situation that you would be confronted with in due course?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff of Travnik civilian protection, although it was prepared for things like elemental disasters, natural disasters, or technologically caused accidents, it also prepared for the case of war and imminent war. We prepared ourselves. And as the neighbouring state was in the throes of war already, that is to say, Croatia was already engulfed in war, we started preparing should war break out in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of plans, and the plans existed. Let me give you an example: We had plans providing for two and a half thousand -- no, five thousand people coming in as refugees. We had that hypothetical. And after the end of the war, 205 [as interpreted] refugees passed through Travnik in actual fact. So you can see the planned figure was 5.000, and look at what actually happened. And we were absolutely never able to envisage such large figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hockic. Since you said that you had staffs in the local communities that you trained and that you had your foremen on the ground, did you train people to perform their assignments in the local communes, the staff in the local communes, and did you try and find the best people for this post of formal manager in the field?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I hear your answer, I would like to correct the transcript. He said they took over 205.000 refugees, whereas on line 2, it says 205. The figure was 205.000. That must be corrected. So the planning catered to 5.000, and they were faced with a figure of 205.000. So it's line 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 205.000. The plan provided for a mere 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the correction made, before the correction was made to the transcript, because the mistake a big one, I asked you whether you made efforts to train the best -- to train the staffs as best as possible in the local communes and the commissioners working on the ground so that they could perform their duties properly.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, our training of the municipal staff of Travnik went hand in hand with our efforts to train the staffs in the local communes and in companies, in firms. And this training, the training I've just mentioned, was for the employees and staff members, and they went to Sarajevo for their training and to Travnik with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the measures that you took to equip and train your employees and the staffs and the commissioners or foremen, did you -- could you, rather, entrust them with assignments and have full confidence in them and confidence in the reports that these people sent back to the staff? Were they trustworthy?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I should like to stress that we waged the right kind of cadres policy in the civilian protection area by selecting professionals, highly moral individuals, hard-working individuals, which meant that these were the right people, and that's how the secretary of defence liked us to select people and deploy cadres for the armed forces, for the police force, and everybody working and going about their ordinary civilian duties and the supply to civilian protection as well. So we trained them, and we believed in these people because they were people trained for situations of that kind. And they were empowered by the law to perform assignments of that kind. So we were one of the very rare staffs who, if I might say so myself, fulfilled the tasks we were given during the war very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have a few more general questions, and then I'm going to show you a series of documents. Tell me this, please: Did the government or war presidency during the war, that is to say in 1993, issue any special assignments to you concerning refugees, the accommodation of those people, assessing the damages, recording property and so on and so forth? So did you receive specific instructions and assignments and orders closely connected to the suffering that war brought about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both the government and the war president of the Travnik Municipality did issue assignments to us of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the war situation you were faced with, did the civilian protection staff of the Travnik Municipality, was it faced with the problem and did it face the problem, the problems that arose, and was it very difficult to fulfil your assignments and go about your work given the war circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very difficult to implement those assignments, and I quoted you one example about the 5.000 people that were provided for on the basis of our plan, whereas in actual fact 205.000 people came in, and we had to deal with that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to ask the usher's help to provide the witness with a set of documents. We have prepared the documents for members of the Trial Chamber and for our colleagues of the Prosecution and the rest of the Defence team and the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, we have 47 documents here of different types. And I'd like to inform you straight away that I'm going to ask you first of all to tell me whether you recognise the document as issued by the civilian protection or relating to civilian protection, whether you recognise a particular document, and then I'm going to ask you some -- about some of your opinions about the events and the facts stated in the documents. But first things first: Take a look at a document numbered Document 30, and the document reference number is 1284. So that's the one we're going to look at first. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the document is entitled "an analysis of the work of the municipal staff of civilian protection of Travnik," dated the 4th of April 1992 to the 7th of the 7th 1993. The date is July 1993. And my first question for you, Mr. Hockic, is whether you recognise this document as being a document of the municipal civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an analysis of the Travnik Municipality civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look at this analysis, which is set out on a number of pages, we see that there are subtitles. And under number 1 we have the area of measures of shelter, of people, of material goods, and second first aid measures, and then we have fire protection measures. Number 4 is the clean up of the terrain or asanacija. Then we have measures to deactivate and destroy the NUS or UXO. Number 6 is measures to protect animals and food of animal origin. Then we have plant and vegetable protection. Number 8 is blackout and cover-up measures. Number 9 is evacuation and taking care of the endangered population and population that has suffered. Next we have the organisation of humanitarian and other activities on the territory of the municipality. After that, we come to cooperation with the UNHCR and other international humanitarian organisations. Reporting is the next chapter. Sessions of the municipal staff of the Travnik CZ comes next. Now, Mr. Hockic, the titles I've just read out to you, are they basically areas of engagement of the civilian protection staff, or do they represent something else or are they something else, something that you Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond could describe to us within the frameworks of that analysis?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, since you're asking me, and you asked me a moment ago how the system of civilian protection functioned, I said that it functioned through self-protection, the measures of civilian protection implemented by the units, special-purpose units, the commissioners, and the service for protecting and saving the population. I'd like to go back to the measures of civilian protection. Everything that you have just set out and that is set out in this document constitutes measures of civilian protection. The municipal staff implemented these measures in the Travnik Municipality. It did so before the war, prior to the war, during the war. And this is, if I can say -- these are our basic tasks, if I can put it that way, in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to take a look at the second heading for first aid, medical assistance. You said a moment ago how difficult it was to plan in advance, and especially to plan for what life would bring with it. Can you tell us, please, in addition to what it sets out here, did the civilian protection staff at one point in time have to face an enormous medical problem and how did it tackle that vast medical problem?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: One of the 16 measures was to provide first aid and medical assistance to people in need in the Travnik Municipality. Preparations in this area were based on assessments of the people under threat, or people needing first aid and medical assistance so that we cooperated with the medical centre of the Travnik Municipality, and we established 12 surgeries in the local communes throughout the Travnik Municipality. We did this because we felt that the citizens should not have to come into the Travnik area, the town itself, because it was being shelled. We felt that it would be a better idea to save the population from being exposed to war and the shelling and so on and stick to the local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to infectious diseases, Mr. Hockic, did you have to face a problem there? And how did you manage? What efforts did you take to prevent infectious diseases from breaking out and dealing with them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: This was a very important area. If you look at just that one year comprised by the analysis, there were over 160.000 refugees passing through Travnik already. And about 30.000 were in Travnik itself, Travnik proper. This was a vast number of people, and we had to see to it that there were the necessary hygienic and sanitary conditions, especially in collection centres. And I can tell you that this was a major problem that we had to face, but we solved it successfully. Let me quote you an example from practice. In 1992, for instance, in the local commune of Kalibunar, in the Jankovici settlement, a typhoid epidemic broke out. With the help of the police, first of all, and I think also the army, we cordoned off the area. The municipal staff decided to cordon off the area, preventing anybody from entering and exiting. And the first aid team -- or the person in charge was Dr. Babic Zdravko of the first aid team in the municipality, and he was given the basic task of dealing with the situation in the shortest possible time. At his disposal, he had doctors from the medical centre in Travnik and the staff of the Travnik hospital as well as the medical staff, the nurses and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, I'm sure that what you're telling us now is very important, but in view of the time we have at our disposal, could you just tell us, please, in addition to these extraordinary efforts made by you, did you manage to suppress and contain the disease and prevent it, and what would have happened had you not taken the steps you took to contain it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did succeed in containing the disease in a record space of time. The president of the commission, Zlatko Pugacic, came from Sarajevo. He was in charge of epidemiology in Sarajevo, and he concluded that we had done the right thing. Had we not done all this, it would have been a catastrophe for Travnik and Zenica, and that was the observation made by Dr. Zlatko Pugacic, who was the principal epidemiologist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to number 1, please. Tell me, Mr. Hockic, do you recognise the document? Let's hear that first.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recognise this document. It is a decision made by the war presidency of the Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document indicate the manner of organisation? And you have answered my questions along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document of the municipal staff. We had 34 local communes. We had 34 civilian protection staffs. But we decided to reorganise them and have 12 staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at document 2, now, please. That's the next one. This is a government document. Do you recognise it? And if so, was this the manner in which the government issued assignments and issued instructions to the municipal staff of the civilian protection of the Travnik Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a government decision and order issued to the civilian protection staff of Travnik, and they worked with us on the basis of an order of this kind. This is one such order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 1 of the order, does that constitute an assignment? And in response to my previous question, would this be in line with what you said, that the care and attention of refugees and putting them up was one of the tasks that your staff had to perform?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. That was one of our tasks pursuant to this order, to organise accommodation and everything else for the refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document I've just shown you, I should like to say for the transcript is -- has the number 1146. The previous document, that is to say, the decision by the war presidency of the Travnik Municipality, is 1097. The analysis that we discussed to begin with, the number of that document was Document Number -- Defence Document 1284. Mr. Hockic, I do this for the record. I repeat those numbers for the record. Let's take a look at the next document, now, Document Number 3. It's not a very good copy, but I hope you'll be able to answer my question; namely, do you recognise the document as being a document of the municipal staff of the civilian protection, the municipal civilian protection staff, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a municipal civilian protection staff document of the Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the preamble to the document, it says that the order was issued by the commander of the operative group of Bosnian Krajina. Can you tell me with respect to the requests made by the operative group, who ordered you to set aside resources -- to take resources for the needs of the army, requirements of the army?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, these were rare situations when we cooperated with the army. We did so on very rare occasions. But as I say, what this applies to was basic equipment and tools that we were supposed to collect for us to be able to perform our basic functions that we were duty-bound to do pursuant to the law. For example, hay forks, hoes and rakes, equipment like that, equipment for digging trenches, picks and spades and axes and so on. We issued receipts and slips, but we used this equipment and these tools to be able to carry out the assignment set us by law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you kept records and receipts of the goods issued, and the people could get the equipment back from you afterwards? Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at document -- well, the previous document's number was 1196. Now, let's take a look at document 4, and its number is 1197, Defence 1197. Tell me, please, do you recognise this document as being one of the civilian protection municipal staff documents?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is of the Municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, at the time, was it necessary for the land to be tilled? Why was this necessary and why were orders of this kind issued?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, Travnik received humanitarian aid from international organisations. However, you saw that there were 160.000 people that passed through Travnik in that year, 160.000 refugees, so it was necessary for us to organise ourselves and to form work platoons in accordance with the instructions that made this quite legal. Such platoons were formed to till the land so that we could produce food ourselves and feed our population and the refugees because we believed that at the time there wasn't enough food obtained from international organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at Document Number 5, Defence Number 1206.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we will have a break now. It's half past 10.00. And we will resume at about 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Benjamin, I believe there's something you would like to say before the witness comes into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution wishes to make a submission. Mr. President, this submission concerns the documents which the Prosecution -- which the Defence intends to tender on behalf of the present witness. Aside from the volume of documents, and I speak particularly to the 12 that I had received translations of earlier on and which -- of which the 12 are basically repetitious, the Prosecution wishes to submit -- or rather questions the relevance of the documents pertaining to the allegations in the indictment against the accused. I do not think, and it is the Prosecution's submission, that this accused does not stand on trial for most of the things that are presented through the documents here today, and it is our submission that in the interests of time, that the documents should not be allowed or should not be admitted at this stage on the grounds of relevance, on the grounds that they are cumulative, and they really do not serve any purpose whatsoever in the advancement of the Defence's case. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to the Defence in a minute, but speaking for myself, the Judges haven't discussed this yet. The Defence has only presented a few documents so far which all had to do with civilian protection. A number of witnesses have made reference to the civilian protection, so documents which are directly or indirectly linked to the civilian protection may seem to be relevant and may help to determine the truth. As far as the issue of admissibility is concerned, as a rule, it is only at the end of the examination-in-chief that this matter is discussed. Would Defence counsel like to respond to the objection raised?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all the documents that we want to show this witness are relevant from the point of view of our Defence for our client. We are showing the difference in the responsibility of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its organs and civilian and other organs. This is something we referred to in our pre-trial brief. You have just mentioned another reason for their relevance. Many witnesses have testified about the tasks of the civilian protection, about the cooperation between the BH Army and the civilian protection. In the course of the Prosecution's case, you yourself expressed the position that it was necessary to know what the competence of the war presidency and the civilian protection and other organs was, and what the competence or responsibility of the army was. This is of exceptional importance for the defence of a commander. If you have a look at the matter, the civilian protection in July 1993 visited all the areas in the Municipality of Travnik and recorded the state of the facilities it found there. The witness confirmed the reliability of their information, and this is linked to counts in the indictment, not just the context that the Defence wants to refer to, the background that the Defence wants to refer to. I'm not going to go through all the documents, but all the documents as a whole refer to the defence situation and the situation that they were involved in, and some of them refer directly to the counts in the indictment that concern destruction and torching. In addition, as far as the admissibility of documents are concerned, if a witness comes -- appears before the Trial Chamber and recognises the documents as documents that he himself drafted or his organ drafted, this shows that such documents are admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Have no other comments to make in addition to the ones made by Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. After having discussed this, deliberated this, we believe that the Defence can continue to show these documents. And when the Chamber is fully present, we will rule on the admissibility of these documents. We will inform our colleague of the issue, and the entire Chamber will render a decision. We have taken note of your objection, but for now we authorise you, we grant you leave to continue showing these documents to the witness. Madam Usher, could you bring the witness into the courtroom, please. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, before the break, we had a look at Document Number 5, number 1206. Could you please tell me whether this is a document from the municipal civilian protection staff and did it have to do with the tasks related to moving into certain buildings on a temporary basis?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the municipal civilian protection staff, and it concerns the tasks that we had in accordance with the law and in accordance with the instructions issued by the Travnik government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 6, Defence Number 1207. The document we have before us, is it an order that the war presidency may have issued to the municipal civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: It's not very legible, but this is a document from the war presidency. And they may have issued such an order in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, was the order forwarded to someone to whom the war presidency shouldn't have issued orders?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think the war presidency wasn't responsible for issuing orders to the 306th Brigade. I don't know why the -- this is referred to in the order, but I think they could issue such an order to the municipal civilian protection staff. We were a civilian body, whereas the other case concerns the army. They had their own command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 7, number 128, Defence Number 128. Is this a document from the municipal civilian protection staff, and does it have to do with the task that you had to clear up the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document from the Travnik municipal civilian protection staff, and this is one of the 16 measures we took in wartime in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 8, Defence Number 1213. And could you tell me whether you recognise this document and is it an order resulting from your obligation to make a list of buildings and commercial buildings in the area of the Municipality of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the municipal civilian protection staff, and this is one of the measures we would take in the course of the war. This is one of the orders that we forwarded to municipal protection staffs -- to protection staffs in local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you tell me the following: It says that this is an inventory of business and auxiliary facilities in Travnik Municipality which have been destroyed or torched. Was it your duty to make an inventory of all buildings, facilities that had been torched regardless of the cause, or did you have any other specific instructions?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The government of Travnik Municipality ordered us to make an inventory of all business and auxiliary facilities in Travnik Municipality which had been destroyed and torched after the clash between the army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the word -- when it says "torched," which is a word which is repeated, this relates to all the buildings that burnt down, not only to buildings that were deliberately torched. Am I interpreting this correctly? You had to make a list of all the buildings that had caught fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether I mentioned this, but the document is Defence Number 1213. Could we please have a look at Document Number 9, Defence Number 1214. And this is a description of residential buildings in the area of Maline, Donja Maline. Do you recognise this document as a document drafted on the basis of the municipal civilian protection staff by a commission that had been formed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the Maline municipal civilian protection, and my signature is here, the 25th of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the third page of the document it, says the 21st of August 1993, you can recognise your signature there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commissions that visited each building and made a list of buildings, did they also have to make a note of any other factors? And if so, what exactly did they have to do? Or rather, did they have to describe any other factors, causes, the time, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Commissions were given the task of making a record of all the buildings that had been destroyed and set on fire in the field, and they were also to make a note of what was important for the protection staff and for the government so that measures could be taken to clear up the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, is this one of the documents and is this a way in which you tried to provide all the information you had obtained about the buildings damaged in the field?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is one way of obtaining the relevant information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, the commission that drafted these reports, how did they obtain information? Was it necessary to go into the field and visit all the buildings, or was this done in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about one commission in one local commune. But in all local communes, all the commissions had the same task. They had to go into the field themselves, and they had to examine the situation in the field and make a record of all the houses destroyed and set on fire. The municipal staff told them to use our representatives in the field. These were professional people who could help them and provide them with the relevant information. Then they could obtain information from the local population who had remained there or who were still present in the surroundings. They made a note of all the information they obtained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 10. It's Defence Number 1220. Tell me whether you recognise this document, and is this one of the ways in which the civilian protection would remove certain items from others?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document from the municipal staff of civilian protection. It's signed by the commander, Momcilo Malenica. And at the time, we had approval of the government or executive committee in Travnik according to which we could seize certain items provided that this was recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hockic, a minute ago you said that you provided information so that measures could be taken. If you establish that someone had misappropriated or committed another crime and that threatened a facility under the protection of civilian protection, in such cases, what sort of measures did you take, if you took any sort of measures?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: There were such incidents in the course of the war. Food was even stolen from our warehouses, from lorries when they were being transported. We took measures, the command of the civilian protection staff took disciplinary measures or referred the case to the police so that they could investigate them. There are written records in our archives on these incidents that occurred in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, could you please have a look at Document Number 11. This document is Defence Number 1221. And then have a look at Document Number 18. 1241 is the Defence number. Have a look at Document Number 19. 1247 is the Defence number.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 11, at Document Number 18, Document Number 19, Defence Number 1247; Document 20, Defence Number 1248; and Document 21, Defence Number 1249. And I would like to ask you whether this is an example or whether this is one of the examples that you mentioned of the measures taken by the civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: These documents are documents from the municipal protection staff. And as I mentioned, it refers to measures that we took when material goods were stolen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 12 - 1255 is the Defence number - and tell me whether this is a document from the municipal staff of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the municipal civilian protection staff in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I show you part of this document, I would like to ask you the following: Since you have spoken of tens of thousands of refugees, Mr. Hockic, tell me, tell me whether at any point in time the civilian protection staff and other organs were confronted with large-scale movement of that population towards abandoned areas and were they confronted with other problems related to this sudden departure from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff of the civilian protection in Travnik, when it received an order from the government in the Municipality of Travnik to move people into abandoned houses and to protect the livestock and agricultural products which were in the houses and by the houses, encountered a serious problem. They were unable to act in this way because people had moved into most of the houses by that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, have a look at paragraph 4, line 1 where you describe some of the information you obtained and tell me whether you yourself were confronted with the facts that you have referred to in your report, in addition to the prohibition of movement for civilians. Can you see that part?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the problem we had to confront. We could only move into a certain number of houses. I see it says 13 houses here. I think it's correct. But as you can see, it wasn't possible to move into 187 houses. People had moved into them before. People were living in very difficult conditions. We had 19 canteens, 10 refugee centres. The living conditions were difficult. And people quite simply left those centres and moved into those houses. We couldn't control the situation. We couldn't prohibit this. They acted in this way before we took any action, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In line 1, it says "a large number of civilians have been noticed who are carrying abandoned property." When they say -- when reference is made to a large number, could you tell us what sort of a number that concerns and what sort of problems did you have at the time? Do you see what it means, "when visiting the field, the commissions determine the following..." and then in line 1, they mention a conclusion that was reached. So could you tell us, at that time with regard to the behaviour of the civilians who were living in impossible conditions at the time, could you tell us what it means when they say that there were a large number of civilians? Were there tens of them, hundreds of them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I think there were hundreds of them. And we couldn't control these people. And the citizens were prohibited from moving around those areas. This was not a prohibition that was respected by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at Document Number 13 now. This is Defence Number 1233. Is this also a document from the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at number 14, Document Number 14. Defence Number 1234. Is this also a document from the civilian protection that relates to one of your tasks?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the civilian protection municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 15, Defence Number 1235, addressed to the Travnik municipal government. Is this a document of yours, and does it also refer to another serious problem that you and other organs in Travnik were preoccupied with at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
