utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the municipal civilian protection staff. It was addressed to the Travnik municipal government, and this is one of the problems we had in 1993. And we wanted to inform the government so that they could take measures and help to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, in July 1993 -- in June 1993, was it possible for food and equipment to be transported to Travnik and to the territory under the control of the army? And to what extent was hunger an issue that wasn't discussed since hunger was widespread? Could you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult to provide supplies and provide humanitarian aid for refugees and for the inhabitants of the Municipality of Travnik themselves. And the municipal civilian protection staff wasn't capable of dealing with this, which is why we contacted the war presidency and the government, to request that they assist us when dealing with this problem, which was very serious, as I said. There was not enough food. Could I just add something else: The UNHCR -- well, we also contacted international organisations for help, primarily the UNHCR, with whom we cooperated. And in 1993, we received 120 tonnes of seed potato and 100.000 bags of various kinds of seeds, and 63 tonnes of -- autumn sowing seeds. I think the UNHCR helped us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at Documents 16 and 17. One is Document 1236, and other one 24 [as interpreted]. Tell us whether these are documents that the government provided to the civilian protection, or are they documents that refer to civilian protection tasks in relation to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Document Number 16 is a government document, the Travnik Municipality. And it charges us with cooperation of this kind. And Document 17 is our own document, the municipal civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at Document Number 22, please. It is Defence Exhibit 1252.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to repeat the last two digits. It is 1236 and 1240, those two documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this brings us to Document Number 22. Mr. Hockic, we already spoke about the commissions that had to establish the situation the premises were in after fighting, after combat. Is this one of the documents compiled in the local commune of Kalibunar?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document of the Kalibunar municipal civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does this document contain the time during which the damage was caused as established by your commission?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now move on to Document 23, and it is Defence Number 1253. Is this a document of the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The municipal civilian protection staff of the Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at Document 24 or 1254 and tell me if these are the steps you took to help in the population's feeding? Because you said a moment ago that the UNHCR had sent you some seeds and other necessary goods to ensure food for the population.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document of the civilian defence staff of the municipality, and this is an order regulating the establishment and formation of a work platoon to engage in farming when it came to hoeing potatoes, weeding onions, and it is in line with what we received from the UNHCR. And the task was to implement this in the local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at Document 25, which is D1256, and tell me whether this is indeed a document compiled by your staff.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a municipal civilian protection staff document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at the document, paragraph 2, which sets out a number of activities. Are these all activities which at that period of time you were engaged in implementing? And what problems did you encounter in going about your business and implementing those tasks?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the activities that we undertook, the measures of civilian protection in the Travnik Municipality, and we had quite a few problems that we had to deal with in the course of our work. The problems we weren't able to solve ourselves we contacted the government of the Travnik Municipality and asked for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document is number 26, number 1263. Is this another document testifying to the work of your commissions in each of the individual municipalities or local communes of the Travnik Municipality that you undertook in implementing the government decision?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is for the local commune called Centar. Centar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hockic, if you had to carry out your tasks close to the front lines, close to the fighting, who issued permission to you allowing you to move around in the area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff of the civilian protection of Travnik would contact the operative group directly, Krajina, and it was located at the command in Travnik at the time. And it would issue permits for us to be able to move around in those areas, in the areas where fighting was going on. But not only for the municipal staff, but also for the commissioners and for members of the civilian protection staff in the local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at Documents 27 and 28, Defence Numbers 1270 and 1271, and tell us, please, whether they reflect what we've just heard from you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. These are documents of the Travnik civilian protection municipal staff, and they talk about what I've just been saying to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at Document 29. D1283 is the number. Before you take a look at the document, however, I would like to ask you this: In case in the local communes there were certain problems, if problems arose, did members of the municipal staff go on the spot to deal with the situation together with the locals there and seek out solutions? Or didn't you -- weren't you obliged to do that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes from an extended meeting of the Stari Grad civilian protection staff. According to our methods of work, this is what we would do. We would have regular visits to the civilian protection staff of the local communes, and we would give them professional assistance and help them in resolving the problems that would crop up on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We've already seen the following document, so we move on to Document 32 or D1302. Is that a document of your staff as well, issued by your staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat the document's number, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is number 32 or 1302.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. That is indeed a document of the municipal civilian protection staff of the Travnik Municipality, yes, sent to the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, take a look at Document 33 or 1303. Is this authorisation from an organ to the Travnik Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: This is a document -- it is a government conclusion, in fact, that is addressed to the civilian protection staff. And it has the force of law, or rather, it is based on the law on the basis of government activity. But at the beginning of the war, we passed a document pertaining to civilian protection for the Travnik Municipality adopted by the war presidency. Yes, it did provide a legal groundwork for us to carry out an assignment like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, faced with situations of this kind, that is to say, when in a given area you had a unit of the BH Army present engaged in an assignment, did you inform those units about the measures you had taken or were about to take? And if so, why did you do that? Why did you inform the unit on the spot about your assignments?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: We were duty-bound to inform units in writing who were active in our area. And we were bound to do that by an instruction on compulsory cooperation which was issued at the beginning of 1992 by the Ministry of Defence. And that's what we did. We acted on it for cooperation purposes, to facilitate matters, and to be able us to perform our tasks, the tasks issued to us by the wartime presidency and the government all in the aim of protecting people and property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document is number 34, it is a government document again, and tell me, please, whether this, too, is a document setting out the tasks of civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. This is the Travnik Municipality government document sent to us, and the conclusion was that it was up to us to solve certain problems in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we're going to look at the next documents, which are linked to your legal duty and given to you by the government to ascertain the state of affairs, to ascertain what condition the houses in your area were in. So the document is Number 35 or D1307. Tell us, please, whether that, too, is one of the reports compiled by a committee set up in the field for the Stari Grad civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it is. It is the Stari Grad civilian protection staff document sent to the Travnik Municipality and the civilian protection staff there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now look at number 36, or D1325 and tell me what that document is about.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: May I just be allowed to add that on Document 35, you have my signature confirming that I received the document myself. It is the Stari Grad civilian protection document sent to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: It says the 27th -- the 20th of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the 20th of July 1993, when you say "7," that is the seventh month, July?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: It is a list of individuals whose houses were burnt down in the area, Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at Document 37, please. Is this also - this document, D1332 - a civilian protection staff document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Travnik municipal civilian protection staff document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the various problems that you had to contend with. Is this then a document instructing you to accelerate the implementation of the orders and assignments issued to you previously?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you that on the ground, the commissions faced a lot of problems and they weren't able to keep the deadline and get everything done within the deadline that we ordered them to do and that the government in turn ordered us to carry out. Now, in view of the fact that the government had asked us to report back to it, that's what we did. We compiled a document, this particular one, asking that the implementation of ordered measures be accelerated regardless of the problems that they were encountering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at the next document, Number 38, or D1337, now, please, and could you take a look at the last page of that document. Can you tell me, please, when the document was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The report was compiled or the document was compiled on the 23rd of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this document, we can see that -- actually, the document is handwritten. Now, why did the chief of staff of the civilian protection staff of Han Bila write out this document in his own hand with pencil and paper? Why is it handwritten?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, as you can see, we had technical problems to contend with, too. There were no typewriters, for example. And as far as I remember, after 11 years, we said at the time, as I myself coordinated this particular measure - I was a member of the staff for fire protection and these were all houses that had been set on fire - we said, all right, if you don't have any typewriters, then compile the report in handwriting. So this report had to be signed and sealed and stamped, and it is a valid document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's dwell on this first document, please, to begin with. On page 1, it says that it is the Pode populated area. Now here, like in other places, was the commission duty-bound to carry out an investigation of each individual house and to write down what it found, what it personally saw on the spot and the information it received about the particular building or premises?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: This commission, like all the other commissions, were duty-bound to go on the spot in the field, go from house to house, and carry out a house-to-house inspection into the condition of the building, and then to reflect that and put pen to paper and write a report. And that's what this commission did, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at page 2. It says "a list of abandoned houses in upper and lower Cukle village." This G and D. What did that mean? It says "G and D Cukle." What does the G and D stand for?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it stands for upper and lower Cukle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the list that follows, is that the list reflecting the condition of the buildings that the commission came across on the 21st of July -- on the 23rd of July 1993 when it inspected the buildings?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was the situation the commission came across on that particular date, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now take a look at the six-page document. It says Rudnik Baje Vrbice inhabited area.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the commission act in a similar fashion identically in setting out all the buildings that existed in that particular locality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think it followed instructions from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the last page, in the B/C/S language, the last place mentioned is Grahovcici. Was that the situation that your commission came across on the 23rd of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Our commission established that the situation was as it was on the 23rd of July 1993 in the populated area of Grahovcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if the front line was quite near and if the fighting was going on nearby, were you able to inspect that particular locality, or rather the locality where there was fighting going on? Were you able to inspect that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was one of the problems we encountered in the field, and we had to ask permission from the army to go there so as not to expose our men to danger. So we had to ask permission from the army to give us permission to go into those areas and establish the situation. That was our cooperation with the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the end of that document, there's a remark. Could you tell us how far the remark had to do with the problem you've just elucidated and commented on.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: In Brajkovici, the army had been billeted there, and we weren't able to perform our task. And we take note of that in this remark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at Document 39 or Defence Document 1344. Is this one of the reports compiled by the commission pertaining to the state of affairs on the 26th of July 1993 in the village of Krpeljici?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is indeed a document compiled by the commission in Krpeljici, and this is the situation on the buildings destroyed and burnt in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This brings us to Document Number 40, or D1345. Tell us what that's about, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: This is a document compiled by the commission of the local commune of Guca Gora. And it is a report on destroyed and burnt-out buildings in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Hockic, is Guca Gora a large village? Do you know roughly speaking how many households there are in that village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: It is a large local commune, yes. How many households? Well, let me hazard a guess. Well, about 200 houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when your commission toured the buildings, went round the village, did it have to make a note of every building and outhouse such as barns, sheds, and so on, auxiliary buildings which might have been destroyed or set fire to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The commissions had the task of making lists of all the houses, all the buildings that were destroyed and burnt, as well as all the auxiliary buildings and outhouses belonging to one household.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this list, Mr. Hockic, as far as I can see, there are 46 buildings inspected by the commission. So tell me now, please, whether this particular commission, in addition to depicting the state of the facility in question, did it also provide you with relevant information as to when the destruction was caused? And pursuant to their information, how the destruction came about in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The commission, just like all the other commissions, did go out to inspect the situation in the field directly. They were assisted by the civilian protection commissioners, and they sent us a report containing all the information they were able to come by when conducting their inspection on the ground. The information they did not have, they could not convey to us, and they could not make a note of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we come to Document 41, or D1346. And tell us, please, what that document is about.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the civilian protection staff of Guca Gora, and it is a report on buildings demolished and torched in the village of Radojicici. The date at the bottom is the 21st of August 1993, and I signed it saying I had indeed received it from the civilian protection staff. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we take a look, for example, at point 3, could we say that the two stables mentioned there belonging to Marko Kafadar were torched on that date, the 21st of August 1993? Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at Document Number 42 or D1347. That's the next document. What's this about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: This is a report compiled by the commission on the destroyed and burnt-out buildings in the village of Velika Bukovica. It is the local commune of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, does this report have a date? Does it indicate the date when these properties were destroyed or burnt?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if it says here that all these buildings were destroyed on the 4th of June 1993, what does that mean? What does it signify to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the report, we see that all these buildings were set fire to and destroyed on the 4th of June 1993. Now, I'm interested in knowing whether you knew what events took place in Velika Bukovica on the 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Trial Chamber's permission, I do not think my friend is quite accurate because there are indications on the list when fires were set on the 9th of June as well. So to indicate to the witness that the fires were set only on the 4th, I think, would be a little bit misleading as the document itself does say that fires were set on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. My learned friend is quite right. And I withdraw that question because I did see that on page 2, there are other dates. So I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Witness, Mr. Hockic, could you tell me, please, whether on the 4th of June the names of the people whose properties were burnt on the 4th of June, to which ethnicity did these people belong to? What was the majority ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: They were all Bosniaks, of Bosniak ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, did your commission provide you with information at that time that the village of Gornja Bukovica was completely destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at Document Number 43, or D1348. Which local commune is concerned here?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: It concerns the Pirota local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at Document Number 44, Defence number 1352.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the civilian protection staff in Guca Gora addressed to the municipal civilian protection staff in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which villages does this report concern?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: It concerns the villages of Bandol, Radojicici, Krpeljici, and Velika Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at Document 1353 now, or Document Number 45. And then have a look at Document 1355, and this document is also Number 46. And have a look at Document Number 1355, which also has the number 47 [as interpreted]. Since we've seen this first document, and you mentioned the villages concerned, do the documents you now see concern an individual list of all the local inhabitants and their families whose houses were torched or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are lists of residents whose houses were burnt in Radojicici, Velika Bukovica, and in the village of Bandol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, since this was part of your responsibility, did you receive from the commission any information as to how many houses remained intact in the village of Bandol, if any houses did remain intact?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The commission informed us that the village of Bandol had been completely destroyed and torched at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Hockic, whether you know anything about fighting continuing in that area, and up until the end of the war, was any damage done to buildings? Were any buildings destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The fighting continued. Buildings continued to be torched. And we were still informed about such cases. But in many cases, we couldn't obtain any information as there was ongoing combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the situation you found there on the 26th of July 1993, and the situation in the year 2000 in the same area, can the situation in 1993 and the situation in 2000 be compared at all?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hockic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I had hoped to conclude my examination sooner, but my colleagues wanted to object to the way in which I was proceeding, and my colleagues wanted to object to showing these documents. So I had to proceed in this manner and go through each document with the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are listening to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add something to my testimony. I forgot to mention that in the course of the war, I also performed other important duties. In 1993, I was appointed by the Travnik district government as a member of the district civilian protection staff for fire protection. So I had this post as well. I had these duties to perform. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We only have a few questions for Mr. Hockic. Cross-examined by Mr. Ibrisimovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hockic, can we go back to Document Number 33 in this bundle of documents. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a conclusion of the government of Travnik Municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date is the 12th of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The 12th of July 1993, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under item 1, it says because of the newly arrived refugees, the municipal civilian protection staff should - and they're referring to the Travnik staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It concerns Grahovcici, Cukle, and Brajkovici. That's the sector concerned. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are all these villages in the Travnik Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the civilian protection must coordinate activities with the 306th [as interpreted] Brigade. This concerns accommodation and reception of refugees?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's an error in the transcript. It says the 306th, and it should be the 314th Brigade, as can be seen in the document. And my last question: On the 12th of June 1993, in these villages -- on the 12th of July, there were buildings which could be used to provide those refugees with accommodation, the refugees who were arriving in Travnik. There were buildings that were fit for accommodation for those refugees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll give the floor to the Prosecution now. We have another 20 minutes until the break. Cross-examined by Ms. Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hockic. My name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin, and I am one of the representatives of the Prosecution in this matter. As the Trial Chamber -- as the President indicated to you, I'll be asking you a few questions. And if at any time you do not understand what I'm saying, please feel free to stop me, and I will oblige. Thank you. For clarification purposes, you indicated to my learned friend that your role was to protect the property and the persons in the Travnik Municipality. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we had to do according to the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you correct me or could you elaborate for me if I'm wrong, do I understand you to mean or am I interpreting it correctly, when you say to protect property and persons, are we talking of life and limb as well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. To protect their lives, too. Because if we had to provide them with medical treatment and if we had to prevent infectious diseases from occurring, et cetera, then that involved protecting their lives as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in addition to that, if I understood you correctly, you were also responsible for protection of fire, anything that had to do with fire prevention. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the civilian protection for fire prevention and also of the regional staff, the regional civilian protection staff fire prevention. So I had these two separate positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my learned friend showed you quite a number of documents. And on each occasion, you stated that this is what the commission presented to me. My question to you is this: You personally have never gone out into the field, have you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I went into the field in the case of the Kalibunar local commune, in the case of the old city centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you will agree with me if I say that the Travnik Municipality is a very wide, broad area? Broad geographical area. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fairly broad area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that you were aware that, for example, in June or, to be more specific, on the 8th of June 1993, there was a conflict in the Travnik Municipality. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I was in Travnik when a conflict broke out between the HVO and the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you just answered my question. The conflict took place between two armies, the HVO and the BiH Army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And as a result of the conflict, a series of things happened: There was loss of lives, destruction of property, to name a few. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you state for the Trial Chamber, then, for me, if as you said earlier on there was a conflict between the ABiH and the HVO, could you state for the Trial Chamber for me: In the numerous documents that you have been shown, how do you know or how you came to find out that these destroyed properties were destroyed by the HVO? And if you want me, if I can find the particular ones where you have highlighted the HVO, this was burnt by the HVO. Could you tell me how you were able to identify which army was responsible for the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, we determined this on the basis of the work of our organ in the field where there was ongoing combat. This was primarily the local communes. The municipal civilian protection staffs followed these activities. And we had agents in the field who also monitored the situation and who provided us with written and oral reports. They would come to the municipal staff, and we would exchange information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, sir, it is your evidence that the conflict was going on between two armies. Am I correct? And it is your evidence that as a result of the conflict, destruction took place. Let's deal with the properties, first. Destruction took place. So my question to you is: If there was a conflict going on between two armies and destruction arose out of that conflict, how could someone -- or assist us, then, how could you assess who was responsible for the damage in light of the fact that you tell us that the fighting was taking place between both parties?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, the war presidency assessed the situation. They were in control of the entire situation in the area of Travnik Municipality. Then the government of Travnik Municipality and the executive committee assessed the situation. And our professional organs, the municipal civilian protection staff also assessed the situation, as well as the agents that we had. These agents had been trained for such things, and this was their task, and they reported to us on the situation that they had observed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I quite agree with you, because that's the report that you received. But I'm asking you now for your personal opinion. What do you understand by what went on -- if a conflict is going on, isn't there shooting on either sides by both armies, throwing of grenades or whatever - would you agree with me - by both armies? Isn't that what was happening? Firing on either side of the line during the conflict? Is that -- isn't that what was happening? Could you answer for the benefit of the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The conflict was between the HVO and the ABiH. That was quite clear. I don't think it's necessary to explain this in detail. But the documents here are valid ones, and they describe the situation in the area at the time. And they describe the measures that we took after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sure that the documents are all very valid; I'm very sure. But I'm discussing this with you from a realistic point of view, reality now. Are you -- is it your evidence that your men, when they went out into the field, was able to determine by I guess people they had spoken to, that -- look, on the 8th of June, that grenade that hit that house over there, that was an HVO grenade, and that one that hit the one over there, that was an HVO grenade? And the houses that were left spared, the ABiH army didn't attack those. Is that what you're trying to say to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The people who were involved in this work, they were from the area. They knew how -- they knew what the ratio was between the ABiH forces and the HVO. They knew where the shells were coming from. They knew how the conflict had started. And in these reports, they ascertained what the situation was in the field and they provided us with this information. And we would provide this information to the government and the presidency, and we would take measures in order to protect this property from further deterioration, to prevent further damage being done to them, and also to protect the population who remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't want to belabour the point, but you will agree with me if I were to say that the reports, in the light that they were presented, were not quite accurate reports, or they could not have been accurate reports given the scenario?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I'd agree that the information wasn't precise, but I think we were able to act on the basis of the information we had, but it's difficult for information to be 100 per cent accurate. But as to what was done in the field, I believe, as a member of that professional organ, that it was done very professionally at the time, given the conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks. Now, as to the ethnic background of the civilians in the Travnik Municipality, I'm sure you'll agree with me if I were to say to you that there were different ethnic backgrounds in different amounts. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your documents, and there were several of them, so I'm not going to really identify any particular one. But in your documents but in the documents that were shown to you by the Defence, when asked what was the ethnic background of the civilians who had lost property, properties that had been burnt and looted and so on, you clearly answered that all the properties, the ethnic backgrounds of the owners of all the properties was Bosniak. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No, there were owners who were Croats and owners of other ethnic backgrounds, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were shown a list, Number 12, 1225 for example, that's just an example. And you were asked "what is the ethnic background of the people there whose properties were lost or destroyed?" And your answer was: "Bosniak." Maybe you could take a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me the order -- the number of the document. Is it 15? 17? It's easier for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's number 12 on the list, and it's 1225.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This concerns the problems on executing the order on temporary settling people in abandoned housing, protection of livestock and agricultural products. People moved into these houses. These were Croatian houses that had been abandoned in the course of the conflict, and refugees moved into them. In order to protect the houses, above all, the houses that people didn't move into, these houses had been torched. They had burnt down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we may have had the document mistaken, because the document I'm thinking of was a list of documents -- houses that you had. Maybe we could look at the latter documents that you just had. It was a pile of documents with a whole list of houses, and when you were asked, you said they were all Bosniaks. And my question to you is --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could help my learned colleague, the numbers are 45, 46, 47, the numbers for these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thanks to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you indicated to us that the ethnic background would have been Bosniak. Am I correct? Now, if according to us or according to as you told us the Travnik Municipality consisted of civilians of different ethnic backgrounds, my question to you then would be, other than the Bosniaks in the Travnik Municipality, did the other ethnic backgrounds -- ethnic-background civilians own properties in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were citizens of other ethnic backgrounds who owned property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive any reports from your commission with respect to destruction of properties owned by other ethnic backgrounds? For example, the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we received such reports, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's just that it wasn't clear to me whether there were properties destroyed by -- as well. So thanks. Now, we move on to life and limb. And you spoke of refugees coming in to Travnik. Could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber enlighten us to the -- as to the ethnic background of some of these people that were coming into Travnik that you had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: On the whole, the refugees who arrived were Bosniaks. I'd like to point out that at the beginning, before the war, or hadn't yet broken out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were also refugees who came from Croatia because there was a war in Croatia. We received Croatian refugees and found accommodation for them on Vlasic in hotels. These were Croatian areas, and the JNA was present on Vlasic. They asked us not to find accommodation for them because they wanted their troops to be accommodated in those hotels, and they asked us to find other accommodation for them. So I mention this because I wanted you to know that we were involved in this matter before the war, too. In the course of the war, most of the refugees were Bosniaks, but there were some Croatian refugees and refugees of other ethnic backgrounds, too. But there were very few of these refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think this might be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's half past 12.00. We will resume at 5 to 1.00. But I'd like to point out that we'll have 45 minutes for you to finish your questions and for re-examination and for the Judges' questions. I'd like to ask both parties to proceed expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is everyone present and correct? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, we -- I thought that we would go into the other limb of your duties which is to protect life and limb. And I first want to ask you -- I'm not going to be too long with you, so bear with me. I first want to ask you, did your unit or your department have powers of arrest? Were you able to make arrests of any nature, kind?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't have those powers. That was done by the police forces in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And was your department solely responsible for refugees?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: That was just one of the 16 measures pursuant to the law that we engaged in during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you had seen persons of a different ethnic background in the Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Travnik there were other ethnicities living there. And in the civilian protection staff, there were people of other ethnicities. And in the local communes, too, there were employees of different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as to the man in the street -- I'll be specific with you. Did there come a time when there were foreigners appearing in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were foreigners on the streets of Travnik as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your unit or your department have in any way to protect the citizens from these foreigners who may have been on the streets of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No, no. That wasn't one of our powers. We didn't do that. That was up to the police, to protect these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that your duties, the protection of life and limb of the civilians, it was -- that duty was particularly limited because you were protecting them only against a certain group of people. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No. We protected all the people. Civilian protection meant protection in natural disasters, accidents caused by technology, and so on, to protect people and property. And of course in war and imminent war, we were there to protect people from epidemics and so forth. But when it came to foreigners, those were police affairs. It was up to the police to see to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I notice that you said your department assisted in the protection of peoples in the course of war or imminent war. Now, in light of that, and I will be specific in the interests of time, the Mehurici area, are you familiar with the Mehurici school, elementary school?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were people detained in that school?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your department have at any time to go to the Mehurici school?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, members of the staff did go. But I was engaged in fire protection, and there was no need for me to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would not have received any reports with respect to the Mehurici school and what may have gone on at the Mehurici school?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: We did not receive that -- or rather, the staff did receive reports, but not reports relating to the school. At least, I don't remember any reports of that kind having come in to the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I ask you this, particularly because you indicated to us that one of your tasks was to provide doctors to attend to sick people, and I know that in the Mehurici school, that service was requested. And I'm asking now, did it come from you? Did you all provide doctors to the Mehurici school?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: In my testimony, I said that during the war we organised 12 makeshift clinics in cooperation with the medical centre, and one of those makeshift clinic was in Mehurici. A member of the staff for medical protection coordinated those activities. It didn't come up within the realm of my own activities so I wasn't informed about that. He would have to be here to answer that question. I'm sure he would know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, sir, correct me if I'm right, then, if I say that you personally did not really go out into the fields, but in fact, you collected -- you based your assessments on -- and your analysis on reports received. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: For the most part, with the proviso that I said in -- I based my work on the town. But otherwise, for the field, I would rely on the reports coming in from the local communes, the commissions and commissioners. So you're right, but just to add that I did go to the urban area, on the spot there of the local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in light of the fact that you indicated to us that the police, as far as you saw your role with respect to protection of life and limb, it did not relate to the police and the police duties? It was completely different. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: [No verbal answer]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness nods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer, please, for the benefit of the transcript. Could you answer, please, your last answer. I think you nodded, but could you give a verbal answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat all that, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had indicated to you that in light of the fact that the police, that you saw the role of the police as the ones who had the powers of arrest and protecting people in those instances, that it was completely different from your role.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Quite different, completely different role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then, you would not -- you would not receive reports with respect to injuries to life and limb in places, for instance, like Mehurici school where people may have been detained?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't receive such reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as such, you really wouldn't be able to assist us today with respect to the detention of people in centres -- in detention centres and such. You couldn't assist us here today?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. President, that concludes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has the floor. Re-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hockic, my learned colleague just asked you a moment ago questions with respect to healthcare, and you said that you had makeshift clinics, one of which was in Mehurici. Now, if the need arose for detainees, for people who had been taken in needing medical care and assistance, was it necessary to inform the municipal staff of civilian protection, or did your makeshift clinic, could it give the medical assistance that was necessary?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: You're asking me a question that doesn't come under my domain. I am in the field of fire prevention. But as I'm a member of the civilian protection department, then this question was discussed collectively. And Mehurici, one of those outposts, probably did provide medical assistance if they were asked to do so. And that's why she is makeshift clinics were set up there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, did you differentiate at all in the assistance you gave to people? Did you differentiate the people? Did you ethnically differentiate between them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No, of course not. We never did that. Never looked at ethnicity. Well, the civilian protection staff was made up of people of different ethnicities, so the same structure was mirrored in the local communes. We didn't look at the ethnicity of anyone. We just extended aid and assistance, regardless of their religion. The important thing was that they were all human beings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, a lot of the documents were signed by the commander -- the staff commander Momcilo. What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, Mr. Hockic, something linked to the previous question asked by my learned friend that you mentioned only some Bosniaks whose houses had been destroyed or damaged or torched. I showed you many reports from Gornja Bukovica, Maline, and so on, other places, too. Who were, in fact, the inhabitants in Guca Gora? What was the population in Guca Gora made up of? Who lived there in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Guca Gora was populated by Croats. That's Guca Gora. But when we talk about the local commune, then that implies a broader area, encompassing other villages, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just have one more question, and it is linked to your care and attention of people who were in the primary school at Mehurici. You said that that didn't come under your work and assignment, and that you were not aware of any information from there. But would you please take a look at Document 21. The third page of that document sent to the public security station --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I just take a moment to find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Document 21, the number, the Defence Number is 1249. And it refers to the 23rd of March 1993, sent to the public security station in Travnik. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I read paragraph 1 of this document, it says the following: "When food was transported for the detainees set up accommodated in Mehurici, Bukovica, and individuals in the Mehurici primary school, there was a lack of supplies when these supplies were handed over to the local commune of Mehurici." Mr. Hockic, does this document speak about your care and attention to supplying food to people in this school, about food to this school?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I have no further questions. I apologise. On page 76, line 14, it says the 23rd of March. Perhaps I misspoke. Perhaps I made a slip of the tongue. It was the 23rd of June 1993. Thank you, Mr. Hockic. I have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No follow-up questions, Mr. President, from us either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Sir, I have a few questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But first of all, I would like to follow on from the question that you were just asked by the Defence. And would you take a look at Document 21, please. It refers to the disappearance of goods that were brought into Mehurici, supplies brought into Mehurici. In that document, Document 21, it states that some of these supplies disappeared. And they are listed. 80 litres of oil, et cetera. And it also says that during transport, and it is Document 1247 now that I'm referring to, 1247, that the supplies taken to the primary school were -- actually, the supplies were being taken to the primary school. Document 1247. Now, look at Document 1241, 1-2-4-1, and it is Document 18, D1241. It is the statement made by the drivers pertaining to the disappearance of supplies. There were two drivers, and they recount what happened. Now, would you please take a look at paragraphs 1 and 2, which state that the goods which were brought in for the local community of Mehurici, for the refugees, and then it says "and imprisoned Croats," "for the refugees and imprisoned Croats." And the second driver states the same thing. The second driver also speaks about the imprisoned Croats. So this is a statement made by the two drivers on the 22nd of June. And that statement is followed by the document of the 23rd of June where the refugees and detainees, where the detainees disappear, and the word that is used is "refugees." Now, how do you explain that? How do you explain the fact that the term "prisoners" or "detainees" has disappeared and given way to the term "refugees"? Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't. Very well. Now, with regard to your authorisation of civilian protection, would you be catering, entitled to cater to people who could be prisoners in a given case? Did you have that responsibility, to bring them in vegetable oil, bread, food in general? Would that come under your field of competence, come within your powers and authorisations?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: From these documents, what I can see is this: That we did indeed take care of that category of persons. However, I think our mandate stipulated first and foremost the care of refugees. But we also catered to the domicile, resident population as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But to the best of your recollections, did you ever focus your attention on prisoners that had to be fed, detainees that had to be fed? So could the army rely on your services to do that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can assume that the answer would be yes, although I didn't work directly with those matters. I was in the fire prevention department, as I say. So this domain is -- I'm on shaky ground. I don't know. Konjaric or someone else was in that post and would know about that better. So I could just assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another point that I'd like you to clear up for us. You have already explained that you studied in Sarajevo and that you studied political science. How come as a political science graduate you find your -- found yourself doing this other job? How was your professional -- how did your professional path lead you to dealing with fires and fire prevention? Could you explain that to me? Unless your mission was a mission of greater responsibility than just looking after fires.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me be more specific. I graduated from the faculty of political science of the social self--- national defence and social self-protection department. So when I specialized, I opted for civilian protection or civil defence. And one of the 16 measures included fire prevention. It wasn't my choice. I didn't go to work there because I wanted to, but because the war presidency thought that I could no longer continue my function as chief of staff, and they sent me to the fire prevention department. I wanted to remain in the civilian protection system because that's where I thought my services could be best used during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, a final question: At the very beginning of your testimony, and the first questions asked you by the Defence with respect to civilian protection, was to know under whom civilian protection came. And your answer was it was under the Ministry of Defence and the supreme organ. And that's on page 22 of the transcript, line 19. I'd like you to confirm that answer, to tell me again. Above civilian protection and organisation, did you have the Ministry of Defence and that that was the supreme authority, the Ministry of Defence, was it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: By law, by the law governing civilian protection, we came under the Ministry of Defence, which means, organisationally speaking, organisationally speaking, we belonged to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All right. But did you depend -- were you independent of the Ministry of Defence and the army? Dependent or independent? If you depend on a structure, then you are in a state of dependency. So were you totally autonomous and independent or were you subordinated to orders and instructions emanating by the Ministry of Defence and by the same token from the units in the field, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: No. We were subordinated in wartime to the presidency and the government. But we certainly did receive instructions from the Ministry of Defence as well because the assistant for civilian protection, the minister's assistant for civilian protection, was in the Ministry of Defence. He was a minister's assistant in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, the Defence provided this voluminous document, long document, stipulating the authorisations to military units, the 306th, for example, the 306th Brigade. To your mind, how could you combine the two, marry the two? A certain form of interdependency with the army, for example, and making an evaluation and assessment on the destruction caused to private property during a conflict? Were you totally independent and autonomous in your establishment of responsibility and assessments of the responsibilities? Do you understand my question? It's rather a complex question and a lengthy one. Do you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I understand your question completely, regardless of the fact it is lengthy. I can say categorically that we were independent, autonomous. But nonetheless, under the command -- not command, but under the authorisational competence of the war presidency of the government. Command is a military term. But we cooperated with the army which we duty-bound to do following an instruction published in 1992, I think, or 1993. I'm not sure of the year. 1992 I think it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And just another small question. You referred to the war presidency on a number of occasions. In your opinion, this entity, war presidency, did it have the competence and authorisation in the military field? Did the -- could the war presidency play a role in military operations, or did it relay this to the competent military authorities? To the best of your knowledge. You might not know about that, but to the best of your knowledge, what do you know about that? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the war presidency assessed both military and political -- the military and political situation. But it did not have any command responsibility in the sense of issuing orders. I don't think the war presidency could issue orders. The army was dependent down the line vertically, down the chain of command and dependent on the commands. That's my opinion anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I have a few questions on the documents that were shown to you. Do you still have the binder with the documents before you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The first binder I would like to ask about -- the first document is Document Number 40. That has also the number 1345.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, this is an investigation about the houses in Guca Gora which have been destroyed and burned out. And what strikes me in this report is that the authors of this report have tried to distinguish between different situations. For instance, in case number 7, they say the house burned down as a result of combat activities. And the same is true for 8. And perhaps also for 10. And in other situations, they don't know, but sometimes they are able to say whether a house has been destroyed after the combat or during the combat. So this is all very helpful and interesting to read. And I have no questions about that document. But I have some questions about another document. That is Document 38, which is in the neighbourhood of Document 40. And that Document Number 38 also has the number of 1337. If you would please take that document.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I have taken it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote it, but apparently these are different authors or a different author from the people who wrote Document Number 40. If you look at page 5 of the document, in the English translation, I don't know what page number -- it's the last page anyhow. You see that the -- yes, you have it? You see that the person or the persons who wrote this make certain remarks on the village of Grahovcici, and they say there: "22 houses were completely destroyed. 10 houses were partially set on fire. And 30 houses were partially destroyed." Now comes my question. When I read this, I get the impression that a distinction is made between destruction and setting on fire of a house. Otherwise, this would not make much sense to say that 30 houses were partially destroyed, and 10 houses were partially set on fire. Have you any idea what kind of distinction is made here between destruction and setting a house on fire?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, the commission's task was to go to the sites. And if a building was completely destroyed, razed to the ground, then they would put the building in that category. If it was partially destroyed, that is to say, if it still had its roof, if its roof and windows were still intact but it had been damaged nevertheless, if it only required repair work, then we would describe such damaged buildings as partially damaged buildings. If a house was partially set on fire, it means that it didn't burn down to the ground. It means that part of it had been burned. Perhaps the roof, the windows, the door, et cetera, but the house could be repaired. So that's how these commissions made these reports, the kind of report that we have before us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So the distinction between partially destroyed or partially set on fire only says something about the cause of the destruction. Was it a fire or was it another event. It is not a distinction, I understand, between destroyed during a battle or destroyed after a battle.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, if the commissions had information from agents of the civilian protection or from staff members, then they would sometimes say that the damage had been done in the course of combat. On the basis of the report, you can see -- well, not in this report but in other reports, when the commission could obtain relevant information, they would make a note of it. Because we asked the commissions to make a note of all relevant information that might be of use, not only for the municipal staff but also for the government and international organisations. And this was in order to be able to carry out repair work and move people into these buildings. As for the information we couldn't obtain from them, well, we asked them to send us any information that they themselves might have gleaned in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: In Document 38, you cannot draw any conclusion from the distinction in terminology other than that. In the case of a house being set on fire, there was a fire, and in the other situation, there was another cause for the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The document was written in the way it was written by the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... to think that set on fire is something that happens after a battle, and destroying things is something that occurs during a battle, but you have explained the importance of the terminology to us. I have one other question: Some of the reports are of July 1993. For instance, this one, 38, is on -- made on 23 of July, the 23rd of July. I take it that the report refers to events in the beginning of June, like other reports of July refer to events in June. For instance, report number 40. About the dates of destruction or the dates of setting of houses on fire, there is some six weeks between the event and the report. How did the committees establish the dates of the reports? For instance, I saw one report in which it was said a house has been destroyed on the 4th of June or the 9th of June, or still another date. What was the information they had to arrive at a precise determination of a date?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that commissions had a lot of problems in the field. We didn't receive the necessary reports on the deadlines that had been set by the government. We informed the government of these problems in writing. And then Mrs. Edina informed me of a certain document or reminded me of a document. There is a document which shows that we asked for civilian protection staffs in local communes to become more involved, and this included this staff, too. We made such requests in spite of the problems they were facing, because combat was still ongoing. So we requested that this work be done. And because of these problems in the field, as you can see in this document which was drafted only on the 23rd of July, well, we insisted on obtaining these documents in spite of all the difficulties. As you can see, this is a handwritten document. There were technical difficulties. We said in spite of these difficulties, draft handwritten documents because there was no electricity, no light, and there were other problems of a technical kind. And because of all of these problems, it wasn't until the 23rd of July that this document was drafted. But what is important is that it was drafted. It wasn't drafted in accordance with our request, but it was nevertheless possible to gain certain insights into the situation and to take measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, what is the family name of Mrs. Edina, if I may ask.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Residovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll give the floor to the parties again. But for the sake of a clarification, or perhaps the interpretation was wrong, you said that given the difficulties, the report was handwritten. I see that the report on Guca Gora, 1345 in the B/C/S version, was typewritten. It wasn't a handwritten report. That's something I wanted to point out. The Prosecution, we have a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have two questions to the witness. Further cross-examined by Ms. Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From light of the President's question on your role, I would like you to look at 1197 and 1196, numbers 3 and 4 on the list. Documents 1196 and 1197. It may be still in front of you. The third and fourth documents on the list. And they both -- they're both orders issued by the municipal civilian protection staff. Agreed? But they're both orders pursuant to an order coming from the commander, Alagic. Would you agree with me if I were to say that your department was in some way subordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how I'd put it: Our commander, Konjevic, attended briefings with Commander Alagic. He was there for the sake of cooperation. Again, I'm referring to the instructions received. But you know, the army follows orders. It was war, and cooperation was established through orders. The presidency issues orders, the war presidency issues orders and would forward these orders to us. It was wartime, and we worked on the basis of orders. And in the case of war in the civilian protection, we also followed orders in spite of the fact that we were a civilian organ. And if there were natural disasters or accidents, we also had to follow orders because that was an emergency situation for the civilian protection staff and for the population. I hope you have understood me. But in my opinion, this was nevertheless a form of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question: Would you say that you fulfilled the mandate that was given to you to protect persons and property in the area of Travnik, in light of the reports that were shown to you by Judge Swart a while ago? Would you say that your mandate was fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: I think we did our work in a very professional way given the circumstances and the conditions under which we had to work. I think we performed our duties, the duties we were assigned by the war presidency and the government in the course of the war because we were a professional organ and our staff members were professionals. And this enabled us to perform our duties in a very satisfactory way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so that leaves room for reports that may not have been accurate as such at times.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, the people working in the local communes weren't as professional as those working in the municipal civilian protection staff. In the municipal staff, we had very good people. That wasn't the case in the local communes. The people working there weren't as professional as those working at the municipal level. And they hadn't been trained in the way that we had just before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a number of questions. Further re-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, in relation to the questions put to the witness by my colleague, you said that in the war certain instructions were often issued as orders; however, the civilian protection, whose orders were the only orders and tasks that you had to carry out?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: We primarily carried out the orders of the Travnik war presidency and the orders of the Travnik Municipality government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now go back to a question that the Presiding Judge asked you. This has to do with you saying that you were part of the Ministry of Defence and that you were under the authority of the Ministry of Defence. Tell me whether there's a difference between the Ministry of Defence, in your opinion, and the supreme command staff of the BH Army? Are these the same organs or different ones?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: These organs are different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of these two organs is a civilian one and which one is part of the military structure?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The command is a military organ, whereas the Ministry of Defence is a civilian one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the role of the war presidency, could you tell me whose duties the war presidency took over? They took over the duties of which civilian organ?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: It took over the duties of the Travnik Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to have a look at a document referred to by the Chamber. This document is Document Number 21. Could you have a look at the first page that you commented on, and the Judge drew your attention to a word, to the word "imprisoned." "They imprisoned Croats in the village of Mehurici." Who are the people who gave these statements? Tutic, Rasim and Sakic, Mujo. Do you know them or can you see who these people are on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: These people were drivers who were involved in the transportation of goods from the main warehouse in the municipal civilian protection staff. They transported goods from that staff to the warehouse of a local commune, civilian protection staffs. And Rasim Tutic is a driver I personally know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at the document dated the 23rd of June 1993. It's the municipal assembly in Travnik, and the other one has to do with the public security station. Do you know who signed these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: The commander of the municipal staff of civilian protection, Malenica, Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: He was the commander, and I was the chief in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is this a professional person who would know what the status of certain individuals was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think Malenica was a professional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, although this is a leading question, you would agree that his familiarity with the situation, individuals that are concerned might be different from the knowledge that the drivers had of these persons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have a look at documents that Judge Swart referred to. The document was drafted on the 23rd of July. I apologise. I'll just try and find the number. The number of the document is 38. It's a handwritten document, and you have already told us why it is a handwritten document. Tell me, please, in relation to this document, what criteria were in force for your commissions in the field when they drafted reports? What criteria did they have to apply?
