Did they have to describe the situation that they would observe when visiting the buildings concerned? Did they have to describe the situation they found in the field when the commission went into the field?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had to go into the field, and they had to describe the situation they observed. But they could provide supplementary information from statements by members of local communes and statements made by our agents in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hockic, if this document is dated the 23rd of July 1993 and describes the situation in various places, does that mean that this is the situation the commission observed on that day in the areas referred to in the document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the situation the commission observed on that day in the area it was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've also had a look at a document concerning Guca Gora and certain other places visited by the commission. Other information was provided there. You have just told me that the commission, when possible, gathered additional information. Could such information refer to various factors, the time of the damage according to the people providing the information, the cause of the damage? Or did such information have to do with the perpetrators? Or was it possible for members of your commission to gather such information, and if they obtained such information, was it their duty to include this information in their reports?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: They had to gather all the relevant information needed by the municipal civilian protection staff, or rather, by the Municipality of Travnik government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also drew your attention to a very important element on the last page of this report, the number of which is 38. In this report and in certain other reports, the following terms appear: "Destroyed" and "set on fire." Could you please explain to all of us, to the Trial Chamber and to all of us, because it's not clear in my mind either, could you tell us whether according to the criteria that you applied it was necessary to have a special list of buildings that had been damaged as a result of fire? If the commission saw that a building was damaged as a result of fire, was it necessary to make a particular note of this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to obtain such information. Some commissions acted in this way; others didn't. I keep mentioning the difficulties that arose as a result of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to a building that had been set on fire, if there was no other information and if there was no information as to the cause of the fire, on the basis of your experience at the time, what could have been a cause or what could have been the causes of such buildings burning down?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Well, this could have been the result of a shell. Someone could have set fire to the building deliberately. The population present in the area could have set fire to a building. Or even the person living in the building could have set fire to the building. I think there were such cases, too, but this is an assumption I'm making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I have understood you correctly, I could say that if it says that a building was only set on fire and no other information is provided, in such a case, the causes of the fire could be various?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HOCKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My colleague has made a suggestion. I don't know how to ask the witness about this unless the interpreters help me. Because apparently in the English text, the word "torched" occurs frequently. So if the interpreters can interpret this word, I would be grateful because it obviously has a different meaning from what the witness just said. And this is why my colleagues have drawn my attention to that fact. I would be grateful if the interpreters could translate the word "torched" into the B/C/S language, because the word "torched" has been used in a number of documents as the translation of the B/C/S word "zapaljen".

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to say that it would be useful to see whether the word used by the interpreter -- by the witness means what torch means. To torch means to deliberately set fire to something, whereas the witness seems to be saying something else. I would like him to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood the semantic problem. It appears that the interpreters have translated what you said into the English word "torch," and this implies that there is the intention to set fire to a building. But when you say that a building was on fire, or caught fire, this doesn't necessarily mean it was a deliberate act. So could you tell us what you mean when you say "a house on fire" in your own language. To help you in French, when you say "a house on fire," this could be the result of a voluntary act or it could happen accidentally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I accept both interpretations. It could be deliberate, and it might happen involuntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that when a document which says "cause of fire unknown," you wouldn't exclude the possibility that this might be intentional or not intentional. It could be both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir, for having come to The Hague. You have answered all the questions put to you by both the parties and by the Judges. And thank you for having helped us understand certain semantic subtleties. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, and we wish you a good trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm addressing the Defence. We have a schedule for next week. It was established yesterday, on the 9th of November, there's an asterisk, which says that this programme is subject to obtaining passports for the witnesses. We won't be sitting on Monday, as you requested. We have Witness 9 on Tuesday, number 59 on Wednesday, 58 on Thursday, and 59 on Friday. Is that correct? I haven't provided the names in case certain of the witnesses will be requesting protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any other information for the moment. We think that all the witnesses listed will be appearing, and none of them have informed Defence counsel that they will be requesting protective measures. But we'll be sure of this when they appear in The Hague. So I believe that the hearings should proceed in an orderly manner as of Tuesday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is nothing the Prosecution would like to say, I would like to thank everyone present in the courtroom, and I will see you all at the hearing on Tuesday at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
